metadata.file_name: Imputing PIRLS s home socioeconomic status from students  and schools  questionnaire data  a simulation with MICE.pdf
metadata.title: Imputing PIRLS’s home socioeconomic status from students’ and schools’ questionnaire data: a simulat

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PIRLS 2021 home socioeconomic status (HSES) and a large set of student and school questionnaire context items, with a simulation-based design that repeatedly imputes missing HSES under different missingness scenarios. For the weighted imputation approach (stdwpmm), the authors incorporate PIRLS 2021 student sampling weights from the dataset (Senate weights via the miceadds implementation), explicitly stating that weights influence both model fitting and donor selection to better reflect the complex stratified sampling design. In the unweighted comparisons, the same MICE framework is run without weight integration, enabling direct comparison of how weighting affects imputation stability and correlation recovery. The paper does not report replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so uncertainty quantification is tied to the multiple-imputation procedure rather than replicate-based variance estimation.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The authors draw a random sample of 5,500 students from the full PIRLS 2021 database (367,575 students total) ensuring complete data on HSES and on the student and school questionnaire variables used as predictors. For RQ1, they introduce missingness completely at random (MCAR) only in the HSES variable while keeping student and school questionnaire data complete. For RQ2, they seed MCAR in both HSES and the 141 student/school questionnaire predictors, then evaluate how well MICE recovers the seeded missingness in HSES only. For RQ3, they retain the naturally occurring missingness patterns in student and school questionnaires at the country/territory level, then add additional MCAR (10%–60%) only to HSES and impute using either PMM (pmm) or weighted PMM (stdwpmm). They exclude the United States, England, and Australia from further analysis because these did not participate in the PIRLS 2021 home questionnaire.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2021 Home Socioeconomic Status (HSES) imputation simulation (student + school questionnaires; Rasch reading score predictors)
main_findings.target_variable: HSES recovery under MCAR (RQ1: missingness seeded only in HSES)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Explained variance (correlation): 36% (r≈0.6) at 10% missingness; 16% (r<0.4) at 60% missingness. PMM best at lowest missingness; all methods show shrinkage (overestimate low HSES, underestimate high HSES). Random forests underperform vs other methods in higher-missingness scenarios.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2021 HSES imputation simulation data with student and school questionnaire predictors and reading literacy Rasch scores, the study leveraged Home socioeconomic status (HSES), reading literacy, and questionnaire context to predict missing HSES values, finding that imputation accuracy (explained variance/correlation) declined from about 36% (r≈0.6) at 10% missingness to about 16% (r<0.4) at 60% missingness. This indicates that higher nonresponse in home SES measures substantially weakens the reliability of SES recovery, so PIRLS contextual data collection and missingness mitigation should be prioritized to protect cross-country comparability.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2021 HSES imputation simulation (student + school questionnaires; Rasch reading score predictors) with seeded MCAR in predictors (RQ2)
main_findings.target_variable: HSES recovery under MCAR with incomplete predictors (RQ2: missingness seeded in HSES and 141 predictors)
main_findings.performance_metrics: At 10% missingness, correlations between original and imputed HSES were similar across methods; RF had significantly lower correlations. As seeded missingness increased to 60%, correlations decreased to around 0.45 for most algorithms; RF dropped to about 0.32 (SE=0.008). Under normality assumptions, stdwpmm and norm methods performed best at highest missingness; stdwpmm showed improved stability when weights were incorporated.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2021 HSES imputation simulation data where missingness was seeded in both HSES and the student/school questionnaire predictors, the study leveraged HSES-related questionnaire context and reading literacy Rasch scores to predict missing HSES, finding that correlations fell from roughly comparable performance at 10% missingness to about 0.45 for most methods at 60% missingness (with Random Forest notably worse at ~0.32). This indicates that when predictor information is also missing, imputation method choice and distributional assumptions become critical, so analysts should not assume that standard imputation will preserve SES relationships under high questionnaire nonresponse.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2021 country/territory-level HSES imputation with real questionnaire missingness patterns (RQ3; additional MCAR applied only to HSES)
main_findings.target_variable: HSES recovery across countries/territories with nonrandom questionnaire missingness (RQ3)
main_findings.performance_metrics: For 10% MCAR in HSES, correlations ranged from below 0.2 (Egypt, Morocco) to about 0.7 (Bulgaria, Hong Kong SAR, Albania, Austria). Correlations did not consistently decrease with higher MCAR, and were higher for countries with more symmetrical (Gaussian-like) HSES distributions and lower missingness in student/school questionnaires. Weighted imputation (stdwpmm using totwgt) improved stability and showed the expected decreasing-correlation pattern with increasing MCAR.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2021 country/territory-level data with real student and school questionnaire missingness retained and additional MCAR applied only to HSES, the study leveraged HSES-related questionnaire context and reading literacy Rasch scores to predict missing HSES, finding that recovery varied widely by country (from <0.2 to ~0.7 at 10% MCAR) and was better for more symmetrical HSES distributions. This indicates that cross-country SES comparisons are sensitive to both distributional shape and the interaction between questionnaire nonresponse and imputation strategy, so weighted imputation approaches should be considered to improve robustness.

data.outcome_summary: This study evaluates whether PIRLS 2021 Home Socioeconomic Status (HSES) can be imputed from student and school questionnaire data using MICE, focusing on how accuracy changes under different missingness conditions. Using a simulation sample of 5,500 students drawn from PIRLS 2021 (with complete predictor records), the authors compare six MICE-based imputation algorithms (PMM, weighted PMM, CART, Random Forest, Bayesian linear regression, and Lasso) and assess recovery using Pearson correlation and explained variance. Under MCAR seeded only in HSES (RQ1), correlation drops from about r≈0.6 (≈36% explained variance) at 10% missingness to below r<0.4 (≈16%) at 60% missingness, with PMM best at low missingness but showing shrinkage (overestimating low HSES and underestimating high HSES). When predictors are also missing (RQ2), correlations decline to around 0.45 at 60% missingness for most methods, while Random Forest performs worse (~0.32, SE=0.008). Across countries/territories (RQ3), recovery ranges from <0.2 to ~0.7 at 10% MCAR, and weighted PMM using totwgt improves stability, highlighting that distributional non-normality and questionnaire nonresponse patterns limit imputation reliability. The paper uses Rasch reading scores rather than PIRLS plausible values for reading, and it simulates MCAR/MNAR-like scenarios rather than estimating causal effects.
